items.summary: Johnson is currently leading Agility through a reverse-merger that is expected to make it the first pure-play humanoid robot company on the public markets later this year. Founded in 2015 by a group of researchers who developed new techniques that allow robots to safely walk on two legs, Agility is trying to capitalize on its lead over a newer generation of AI-inspired robotic startups like Figure, 1X, the Bot Company, or Sunday Robotics. Digit operates in a human-free space right now, but the version 5, expected to be unveiled this fall, will have the ability to sense humans and won’t need to be kept in a robot-only zone. [...] While Agility doesn’t have Tesla’s capital, it does have a robot, Digit, that is already useful in the real world. The robot is already generating revenue, carrying totes and bins in manufacturing and warehouse settings for customers like Amazon, GXO, Schaeffler, and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. items.title: Robots Are Coming — But Not Everywhere
items.summary: “The ChatGPT moment for robotics is coming,” declared Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the Consumer Electronics Show in January 2025. items.title: WOW! Social media captures everything and has alerts 🚨
items.summary:
WOW! Social media captures everything and has alerts 🚨 

I’m not sure how to feel about this. What are your thoughts?

This 22 year-old, third grade student teacher posted a Snapchat that got her arrested in no time! 

Incident Overview
•The Post: Written by 22-year-old student-teacher Kristen Volpe while working on a third-grade lesson plan at John L. Hensey Elementary School in Washington, Illinois.  She posted this message asking, "I was halfway through my lesson plan and one of my students pressed the power button on my computer lesson plan is gone chat do I sh00t the child or just the whole school". 
•The Context: Volpe stated the message was an exasperated joke sent via Snapchat to a private group chat with just three people (her boyfriend and two roommates) after a student turned off her computer and erased her work. 
•The Flag and Arrest: Snapchat’s automated safety/AI monitoring flagged the wording and reported it to the FBI, who then notified the Tazewell County Sheriff's Office. Deputies arrived at the school and arrested her within an hour of the message.
•The Outcome: Volpe was booked for disorderly conduct, and the charges were later dropped after she completed a deferred prosecution program.

items.title: She's 27. Works a forge — hot metal, rollers, a shop that glows orange all shift.
items.summary:
She's 27. Works a forge — hot metal, rollers, a shop that glows orange all shift.

Last month: ~$4,500 in wages, ~$5,000 from filming it.

Here's the strange part. 

The most replayed moment in her videos isn't the fire or the machines. It's a one-second close-up of her face covered in soot.

Think about what that shot competes against. 

The entire feed is optimized faces — filters, ring lights, skincare routines, a billion-dollar industry devoted to looking flawless. 

And in the middle of it: a face that just did eight hours of real work. It stops people cold, because it's the one thing in the feed that isn't asking to be liked.

The dirt is the receipt. 

No caption could prove what that one second proves.

Fire does the rest. 

Humans have stared at glowing metal for thousands of years — the scroll just made it vertical. 

Her backdrop is the oldest attention magnet on earth, and she gets it free with the shift.

She films almost nothing on purpose. 

The phone stands at the edge of the station, the shift happens. 

AI picks the moments, cuts them, writes the hooks, schedules the week. 

Her editing time: zero.

At 120K followers, workwear and safety gear brands pay $1,500-3,000 per integration — gloves, boots, eyewear shown doing their actual job in real heat. 

Affiliate links on that same gear earn around the clock. 

Platform payouts stack underneath.

The shop didn't change. 

The heat didn't change. 

She just stopped washing the proof off before anyone saw it.

Every job leaves marks like that — dust, calluses, burns, paint. Most people hide them. 

On camera, they're the most convincing thing you own.

items.title: 11 LLM evaluation methods AI engineers must know:
items.summary:
11 LLM evaluation methods AI engineers must know:

(bookmark this)

Two eval metrics can rank the same two models in opposite orders, and neither one is wrong.

A model that paraphrases the reference can score near zero on BLEU and near the top on BERTScore for the exact same output.

Neither metric is wrong because one is measuring wording and the other is capturing meaning.

This is why LLM evaluation is fragmented into several methods, depicted in the visual below and grouped by what each one assumes:

> Reference-based (ground truth exists):

- BLEU
- ROUGE
- BERTScore

> Judge-based (no ground truth):

- G-Eval
- LLM-as-Judge
- LLM juries

> Human and deterministic:

- Human eval
- DAG

> Built for agents:

- Trajectory accuracy
- Multi-turn eval

> Run as a gate:

- Safety eval

To use them in practice, most of these metrics are already implemented in Opik, which is open source (20k+ stars) and runs them over traced production data. You can start using them in a few lines of code.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/vahjkkfJCt

(don’t forget to star it ⭐️)

That said, metrics only point at the failing case.

The rest of the work is still done manually, like inspecting the trace to see where the span went wrong, editing a prompt or a tool description, re-running, and checking that the fix did not break anything else.

My co-founder wrote a walkthrough (with code) that automates this loop using Opik.

It explains the full lifecycle where a failing trace gets diagnosed, the fix runs against the exact input that failed, and that input stays in the eval set as a regression case so it does not recur.

Read it below.
